5-6.6.2 
Testing. 
Testing should be done regularly to insure that COC, chemical levels, and bacteria 
levels are within the targeted control range. This requirement could demand a testing 
frequency of three times per week, or even daily. 
5-6.7 
Cooling Tower Operator Duties. 
If detected early, problems associated with scaling, corrosion and fouling in a cooling 
tower system can be minimized by corrective action. Some of the things the operator 
should look for when on-site are described below. 
5-6.7.1 
Cooling Tower Distribution Deck. 
It is important to look for the presence of algae, debris, or anything that has plugged 
water distribution holes causing an uneven water flow through the tower, thus lowering 
tower efficiency. Clean plugged holes and replace damaged water distribution spray 
nozzles. In addition, look for the presence of algae deposits. If algae deposits are 
present, increase the level or frequency of biocide or algaecide treatment, and cover the 
deck if uncovered. 
5-6.7.2 
Cooling Tower Fill, Air Intake Slats, and Basin. 
5-6.7.2.1 
Scale Deposits on Cooling Tower Fill. 
The presence of deposits, particularly on cooling tower fill, can be established by 
removing some fill to determine if partial plugging has occurred. Scale can range in 
color from white to gray or reddish depending on the scale composition. Scale formation 
on the cooling tower fill usually indicates a severe scaling situation. If possible, obtain a 
sample of the scale for analysis and, based on the result, select a scale inhibitor for that 
specific scale. 
5-6.7.2.2 
Scale Deposits on Air Intake Slats. 
Scale can form on the air intake slats of a cooling tower. This buildup is due mostly to 
water splashing and evaporating, causing deposition of soluble salts or minerals. This 
situation does not indicate a serious problem. These deposits can be, and should be, 
washed off periodically, but ideally not into the cooling tower basin. Chemical treatment 
can provide some reduction in the occurrence deposits. 
5-6.7.2.3 
Slime Deposits. 
Slime deposits (microbiological) can sometimes be detected by feeling below the water 
level on the distribution deck and on the walls of the cooling tower basin. Most 
microbiological growth will have a slimy feel. If slime deposits are present, increase 
biocide frequency or increase the dosage. 
 
 

=== 2023 PDF Page 166 ===
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
144 
5-6.7.2.4 
Suspended Solids. 
The purpose of a dispersant is to keep particulate solids in suspension and to prevent 
them from settling or from adhering to heat transfer surfaces. Adequate water flow is 
required to prevent them from settling. Particulate solids in suspension are removed 
with the blowdown water. The tower water should be turbid if the dispersant is doing its 
job. Keep the cooling tower sump clean of SS by cleaning periodically and using a filter. 
5-6.7.3 
Corrosion Test Coupons. 
When removing corrosion coupons, always note and record the visual appearance with 
regard to the presence of scale, rust, or biomass. Take photographs of the corrosion 
coupons. Submit (or evaluate) coupons for corrosion rate and for the type of corrosion 
that is occurring. 
5-6.7.4 
Inside Surface of Heat Exchanger Tubes. 
To effectively examine the inside (water-contacted) surfaces of heat exchanger tubes, a 
boroscope is needed because only a few inches of the interior can be seen visually 
using a flashlight. Scale deposits, typically hard and tightly adhered to the tube surface, 
range in color from white to gray or reddish, depending on the composition of the scale. 
No scale should be present. It is important to inspect heat exchanger tubes at least 
once per year. 
Fouling-type deposits may look similar to scale deposits. Unlike scale, these deposits 
usually adhere loosely to the tube surface. Biomass will appear slimy and feel slippery, 
and will usually adhere loosely. 
5-6.7.5 
Chiller Performance. 
Degradation of chiller performance or chiller efficiency may be a strong indication of 
scale or fouling problems in the chiller. If a reduction in chiller capacity occurs while 
cooling water is being cooled efficiently and within design parameters, then the chiller 
condenser section should be opened and examined. The chiller evaporator section may 
not contain water material scale but may be fouled with corrosion products. You should 
open and examine the chiller evaporator if chilled water could possibly be inadequately 
treated. 
5-6.7.6 
Cooling Tower Surfaces. 
Cooling towers made of galvanized steel should be examined for white rust or possible 
rusty surfaces that may indicate that the galvanizing is no longer present on the metal 
surfaces and the steel is rusting. Cooling towers constructed of wood should be 
examined for wood deterioration or decay.

5-7 
COOLING WATER SYSTEM START-UP AND LAYUP 
REQUIREMENTS. 
The startup of a new cooling water system requires special consideration. Proper 
cooling water system layup is also important, especially for chiller tube bundles or other 
heat exchange equipment. For a new cooling tower system, it is important to make sure 
that the equipment that contacts the cooling water is clean and properly protected from 
initial corrosion. Also, disinfection is needed to eliminate the presence of microbiological 
organisms that can cause corrosion, deposits, and growth of pathogenic organisms 
such as Legionella bacteria. Implementation of a proper layup process is critical to 
prevent corrosion and microbiological growth during stagnant water conditions. 
5-7.1 
Stand-by Conditions. 
The term “stand-by” is often applied to a chiller that is in rotation with other chillers on-
line. This stand-by period could be of varying duration, from a few days to a few weeks. 
Rotating chillers frequently is important for minimizing stagnant conditions that lead to 
under-deposit and MIC corrosion. It is good practice to run the recirculation pumps 
through a stand-by chiller for at least 15 minutes each day to minimize corrosion. A 
chiller that must be left on stand-by for an extended period of weeks without 
recirculation should be laid up wet or dry according to procedures described in 
paragraph 5-7.4. 
5-7.2 
Common Problems during Layup or Due to Improper Initial Start-up. 
Common problems that occur during layup or due to improper initial start-up include 
corrosion of tubes and transfer piping (sometimes to the point of failure), micro- 
biological growth with potential for MIC corrosion, and growth of pathogenic 
microorganisms. 
5-7.3 
Start-up of New Cooling Water Tower Systems. 
5-7.3.1 
Initial Cleaning. 
A new cooling water tower system will contain dirt, oils, greasy films, and rust located on 
the metal surfaces as a result of system fabrication. A pre-operational alkaline cleaning 
process is required to remove the dirt, oil, grease, and rust, and to prepare metal 
surfaces for initial corrosion control. When galvanized steel is involved, special care 
must be taken so that the pH does not exceed 8.5 during the cleaning and passivation 
process to avoid conditions that promote white rust. The cleaning and passivating 
procedure for a new cooling tower system is usually part of a new system construction 
project and, as such, is not in the direct control of the cooling system operations 
personnel. Verification of the completion of these important steps is obtained from the 
contracting officer involved with the project. A cleaning and passivation procedure for 
cooling tower systems with galvanized steel is provided below. The procedure is similar 
for systems that do not contain galvanized steel, except that the pH restriction does not 
apply. 
 
 

=== 2023 PDF Page 168 ===
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
146 
5-7.3.2 
Cleaning and Passivation Procedures. 
In the startup of new cooling tower systems containing complex metallurgies that 
include galvanized steel, follow the cleaning and passivation procedures for cooling 
tower systems containing galvanized steel, stainless steel, mild steel, or copper. These 
procedures should not be used for cleaning and passivating aluminum. Conventional 
chemical cleaners and typical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) water 
treatment programs use highly alkaline, high-pH water, which can initiate white rust 
formation on galvanized surfaces and copper tubes. Galvanized steel can simply be 
passivated by exposure to highly aerated water and a phosphate or polysilicate 
treatment. This treatment forms a zinc corrosion inhibition layer, which is a natural, 
dense, adherent, and protective corrosion product film. High pH (above 8.5) produces 
unwanted white rust that is fragile and not protective against corrosion. The following 
procedures are recommended. 
5-7.3.2.1 
Hydrostatic Testing. 
Perform hydrostatic testing: 
a. Inspect and remove all debris. 
b. Fill the system with treated water and circulate. This should include 
orthophosphate or hexametaphosphate (as PO4) at 40 to 60 ppm, and 
tolyltriazole (active) at 10 to 20 ppm. 
5-7.3.2.2 
Pre-operational Cleaning Procedure. 
If the system passes hydrostatic testing, proceed immediately to this pre-operational 
cleaning and passivation procedure. Do not allow untreated water to be added to the 
system. 
a. Drain and flush any debris from hydrostatic testing. 
b. Dose and circulate (for 24 hours) a sufficient amount of a cleaning formula 
based on the volume of the system. A formulation is provided below. 
c. Drain and flush the system, and clean all strainers. 
d. Fill the system with makeup water and circulate for 30 minutes. 
e. Take a sample of system water while it is circulating. The sample should 
match the makeup water supply for clarity and SS; conductivity ±10 percent; 
and pH ±0.3 pH units from 7.5 to 8.5. 
If necessary, repeat steps a) through e) until the system water matches this description. 
The system should now be clean and passivated. 
5-7.3.2.3

Apply this chemical cleaning and passivation formulation when the water system pH is 
7.5 to 8.5; adjust pH as required. Formulation limitations may require adding separate 
components to keep things in solution. Other formulations may be used.

APPENDIX A PRACTICAL (PUCKORIUS) SCALING INDEX (PSI) 
A-1 
DEVELOPMENT OF PSI. 
Have been used to predict the tendency of water to form or dissolve scale. Both the LSI 
and the RSI are based on the pH of saturation (pHs) for calcium carbonate under a 
specific water condition. Both indices use the measured pH of the cooling water. 
1. LSI = (measured pH) - (pHs). A positive value indicates scale; a negative 
value indicates no scale. 
2. RSI = (2 pHs) - (measured pH). A value below 6 means scale; above 6 
means no scale. 
A-1.1 
PSI. 
Use of LSI and RSI sometimes gave inconsistent or even conflicting results. Based on a 
long-term study relative to calcium carbonate scale formation when applying both the 
LSI and RSI, P.R. Puckorius and J.M. Brooke developed a new index that gives much 
better and more consistent indication of cooling water-scaling conditions. The new 
index, the Practical Scaling Index (PSI), sometimes called the Puckorius Scaling Index, 
is based on correcting the system pH to match the total alkalinity of the water being 
evaluated. This is necessary because the pH is often buffered, causing the pH to relate 
incorrectly to the bicarbonate alkalinity, one of the factors in the pHs calculation. 
A-2 
CALCULATING PSI. 
To calculate the PSI, the pHs is determined in the same manner as for the LSI and RSI. 
An adjusted or equilibrium pH (pHeq) is obtained from a total alkalinity/pH chart (Table

𝐏𝐏𝐏𝐏𝐏𝐏 = (𝟐𝟐 𝐩𝐩𝐩𝐩𝐬𝐬) − (𝐩𝐩𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐞𝐞𝐞) 
A value below 6 means scale; above 6 means no scale.

water. The following factors and formula are used in determining the pHs:

C = Calcium hardness (ppm as CaCO3) (Table A-3)

DEFINITION OF TERMS. 
Acid:  A compound, usually having a sour taste, which can neutralize an alkali or base; 
a substance that dissolves in water with a formation of hydrogen ions. 
Aeration:  Intimate contact between air and liquid by one of the following methods: 
spraying the liquid in the air; bubbling air through the liquid; or agitating the liquid to 
promote surface absorption of air. 
Algae:  Tiny plant life, usually microscopic, existing in water. They are mostly green, 
blue-green, or yellow-green, and are the cause of most tastes and odors in water. They 
create suspended solids (SS) when they grow in an industrial water system. 
Alkalinity:  (a) A term used to represent the content of carbonates, bicarbonates, 
hydroxides, and occasionally borates, silicates, and phosphates in water. (b) The 
capacity of water to react with hydrogen ions. 
Alkalinity, total or mixed indicator (M):  A measure of the total alkalinity of water. 
Measured by the quantity of 0.02 normality (N) sulfuric acid required to bring water to 

Page 268:
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
246 
pH of 4.4, as indicated by the change in color of methyl orange or a mixed indicator. 
Results are expressed in parts per million (ppm) as calcium carbonate. 
Alkalinity, Phenolphthalein (P):  A measure of hydroxide ions (OH) plus one-half of 
the normal carbonates in water. Measured by the quantity of 0.02 normality (N) sulfuric 
acid required to bring the water to pH 8.2, as indicated by the de-colorization of 
phenolphthalein indicator. Results are expressed in parts per million (ppm) as calcium 
carbonate. 
Alkalinity, Hydroxyl:  A measure of hydroxyl ion (OH-) contribution to the alkalinity. 
This is related to the system pH and also may be referred to as “causticity.” 
Backwash:  The reversal of flow through a filter or an ion exchanger to wash clogging 
material out of the filtering medium and reduce conditions causing loss of head. 
Backflow preventer:  A device for a water supply pipe to prevent the backflow of water 
into the water supply system from the system which it supplies. 
Bacteria:  Simple single-cell microscopic organisms generally free of pigment. They do 
not require light for their life processes. 
Base:  An alkali or hydroxide of alkali metals and ammonia. They can neutralize acids 
to form salts and water. A base will ionize to form hydroxyl ions (OH). 
Biocides:  Material typically used to destroy microorganisms (also called 
“microbiocides”). 
Biological Deposits:  Water-formed deposits of organisms or the products of their life 
processes. Biological deposits may be composed of microscopic organisms, as in 
slimes, or of macroscopic organisms such as barnacles or mussels. 
Blowdown:  Draining a portion of water from a system to reduce the concentration of 
dissolved solids or to discharge accumulations of materials carried by the water. 
British Thermal Unit (BTU):  The amount of heat necessary to raise the temperature of 
one pound of water one degree Fahrenheit (°F). 
Brine:  A saturated solution for ion exchange regeneration, refrigeration, or cooling 
processes. It is usually a sodium chloride water solution for ion exchange regeneration. 
It may be sodium chloride water solution or calcium chloride water solution for 
refrigeration. 
Causticity:  A common term that describes hydroxyl alkalinity or the alkalinity resulting 
from the presence of the hydroxyl ion (OH). 
Concentration:  A measure of the amount of dissolved substances contained per unit 
volume of solution. This may be expressed as grains per gallon, pounds per million 
gallons, milligrams per liter, ppm, or percent. 

Page 269:
UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
247 
Condensate:  The material formed when vapor returns to the liquid state. In steam 
heating systems, the water condensed from steam. In air conditioning, water extracted 
from air by condensation on the cooling coil of a refrigeration machine. 
Conductivity, Specific Conductance:  The reciprocal of the resistance in ohms 
measured between opposite faces of a centimeter cube of an aqueous solution at a 
specified temperature. Electrical conductivity is expressed in micromhos (µmhos), the 
reciprocal of megohms. This is used as a measure of total dissolved solids (TDS). 
Corrosion:  The destruction of a substance, usually a metal, or its properties because 
of a reaction with its (environmental) surroundings. 
Cycles of Concentration (COC):  In a system in which water lost through evaporation 
and blowdown is replaced with makeup water, COC is the ratio of the makeup quantity 
to the blowdown quantity (COC = M/B). It is the number of times the makeup water is 
concentrated in the system. The COC can also be calculated by dividing either the 
conductivity or the chloride content of the blowdown by the conductivity or chloride 
content of the makeup (COC = Condbd/Condmw). 
Deaerator:  Device for removing non-condensable gases from the boiler. It may operate 
on the principle of either heat or vacuum. 
Dealkalization:  Exchange of bicarbonate for chlorides in an ion exchange process. 
Deionization:  Complete removal of ions from water. 
Demineralization:  Reduction of the mineral content of water by a physical or chemical 
process; removal of salts. 
Disinfection:  The process of killing most (but not necessarily all) of the harmful and 
objectionable microorganisms in a fluid by various agents such as chemicals, heat, 
ultraviolet light, ultrasonic waves, or radiation. 
Dissolved solids:  (a) Solids, usually minerals, which are present in solution. (b) The 
dried residue from evaporation of the filtrate after separation of suspended solids (SS).

5-6.6.1 
Treatment. 
Medium and large cooling towers are usually, but not always, treated with a liquid 
formulation containing both scale inhibitors and corrosion inhibitors. These are often 
simply referred to as an "inhibitor.” Inhibitor products are usually fed on a continuous 
basis using automated control and feed equipment. The concentration of these 
formulated products varies greatly from vendor to vendor. Biocides are usually, but not 
always, liquid products. It is common to use an oxidizing biocide as a primary biocide 
and a non-oxidizing biocide as a secondary biocide, used as needed to control bacteria 
and other biological growth. Oxidizing biocides can either be fed continuously at a low 
level or dosed periodically at a higher level. Non-oxidizers are dosed as needed and 
only when oxidizing biocides are either ineffective or not used at all. 

UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
143 
5-6.6.2 
Testing. 
Testing should be done regularly to insure that COC, chemical levels, and bacteria 
levels are within the targeted control range. This requirement could demand a testing 
frequency of three times per week, or even daily. 
5-6.7 
Cooling Tower Operator Duties. 
If detected early, problems associated with scaling, corrosion and fouling in a cooling 
tower system can be minimized by corrective action. Some of the things the operator 
should look for when on-site are described below. 
5-6.7.1 
Cooling Tower Distribution Deck. 
It is important to look for the presence of algae, debris, or anything that has plugged 
water distribution holes causing an uneven water flow through the tower, thus lowering 
tower efficiency. Clean plugged holes and replace damaged water distribution spray 
nozzles. In addition, look for the presence of algae deposits. If algae deposits are 
present, increase the level or frequency of biocide or algaecide treatment, and cover the 
deck if uncovered. 
5-6.7.2 
Cooling Tower Fill, Air Intake Slats, and Basin. 
5-6.7.2.1 
Scale Deposits on Cooling Tower Fill. 
The presence of deposits, particularly on cooling tower fill, can be established by 
removing some fill to determine if partial plugging has occurred. Scale can range in 
color from white to gray or reddish depending on the scale composition. Scale formation 
on the cooling tower fill usually indicates a severe scaling situation. If possible, obtain a 
sample of the scale for analysis and, based on the result, select a scale inhibitor for that 
specific scale. 
5-6.7.2.2 
Scale Deposits on Air Intake Slats. 
Scale can form on the air intake slats of a cooling tower. This buildup is due mostly to 
water splashing and evaporating, causing deposition of soluble salts or minerals. This 
situation does not indicate a serious problem. These deposits can be, and should be, 
washed off periodically, but ideally not into the cooling tower basin. Chemical treatment 
can provide some reduction in the occurrence deposits. 
5-6.7.2.3 
Slime Deposits. 
Slime deposits (microbiological) can sometimes be detected by feeling below the water 
level on the distribution deck and on the walls of the cooling tower basin. Most 
microbiological growth will have a slimy feel. If slime deposits are present, increase 
biocide frequency or increase the dosage. 
 
 

UFC 3-230-13 
1 March 2023 
 
144 
5-6.7.2.4 
Suspended Solids. 
The purpose of a dispersant is to keep particulate solids in suspension and to prevent 
them from settling or from adhering to heat transfer surfaces. Adequate water flow is 
required to prevent them from settling. Particulate solids in suspension are removed 
with the blowdown water. The tower water should be turbid if the dispersant is doing its 
job. Keep the cooling tower sump clean of SS by cleaning periodically and using a filter. 
5-6.7.3 
Corrosion Test Coupons. 
When removing corrosion coupons, always note and record the visual appearance with 
regard to the presence of scale, rust, or biomass. Take photographs of the corrosion 
coupons. Submit (or evaluate) coupons for corrosion rate and for the type of corrosion 
that is occurring. 
5-6.7.4 
Inside Surface of Heat Exchanger Tubes. 
To effectively examine the inside (water-contacted) surfaces of heat exchanger tubes, a 
boroscope is needed because only a few inches of the interior can be seen visually 
using a flashlight. Scale deposits, typically hard and tightly adhered to the tube surface, 
range in color from white to gray or reddish, depending on the composition of the scale. 
No scale should be present. It is important to inspect heat exchanger tubes at least 
once per year. 
Fouling-type deposits may look similar to scale deposits. Unlike scale, these deposits 
usually adhere loosely to the tube surface. Biomass will appear slimy and feel slippery, 
and will usually adhere loosely. 
5-6.7.5 
Chiller Performance. 
Degradation of chiller performance or chiller efficiency may be a strong indication of 
scale or fouling problems in the chiller. If a reduction in chiller capacity occurs while 
cooling water is being cooled efficiently and within design parameters, then the chiller 
condenser section should be opened and examined. The chiller evaporator section may 
not contain water material scale but may be fouled with corrosion products. You should 
open and examine the chiller evaporator if chilled water could possibly be inadequately 
treated. 
5-6.7.6 
Cooling Tower Surfaces. 
Cooling towers made of galvanized steel should be examined for white rust or possible 
rusty surfaces that may indicate that the galvanizing is no longer present on the metal 
surfaces and the steel is rusting. Cooling towers constructed of wood should be 
examined for wood deterioration or decay.

1 March 2023 
 
145 
5-7 
COOLING WATER SYSTEM START-UP AND LAYUP 
REQUIREMENTS. 
The startup of a new cooling water system requires special consideration. Proper 
cooling water system layup is also important, especially for chiller tube bundles or other 
heat exchange equipment. For a new cooling tower system, it is important to make sure 
that the equipment that contacts the cooling water is clean and properly protected from 
initial corrosion. Also, disinfection is needed to eliminate the presence of microbiological 
organisms that can cause corrosion, deposits, and growth of pathogenic organisms 
such as Legionella bacteria. Implementation of a proper layup process is critical to 
prevent corrosion and microbiological growth during stagnant water conditions. 
5-7.1 
Stand-by Conditions. 
The term “stand-by” is often applied to a chiller that is in rotation with other chillers on-
line. This stand-by period could be of varying duration, from a few days to a few weeks. 
Rotating chillers frequently is important for minimizing stagnant conditions that lead to 
under-deposit and MIC corrosion. It is good practice to run the recirculation pumps 
through a stand-by chiller for at least 15 minutes each day to minimize corrosion. A 
chiller that must be left on stand-by for an extended period of weeks without 
recirculation should be laid up wet or dry according to procedures described in 
paragraph 5-7.4. 
5-7.2 
Common Problems during Layup or Due to Improper Initial Start-up. 
Common problems that occur during layup or due to improper initial start-up include 
corrosion of tubes and transfer piping (sometimes to the point of failure), micro- 
biological growth with potential for MIC corrosion, and growth of pathogenic 
microorganisms. 
5-7.3 
Start-up of New Cooling Water Tower Systems. 
5-7.3.1 
Initial Cleaning. 
A new cooling water tower system will contain dirt, oils, greasy films, and rust located on 
the metal surfaces as a result of system fabrication. A pre-operational alkaline cleaning 
process is required to remove the dirt, oil, grease, and rust, and to prepare metal 
surfaces for initial corrosion control. When galvanized steel is involved, special care 
must be taken so that the pH does not exceed 8.5 during the cleaning and passivation 
process to avoid conditions that promote white rust. The cleaning and passivating 
procedure for a new cooling tower system is usually part of a new system construction 
project and, as such, is not in the direct control of the cooling system operations 
personnel. Verification of the completion of these important steps is obtained from the 
contracting officer involved with the project. A cleaning and passivation procedure for 
cooling tower systems with galvanized steel is provided below. The procedure is similar 
for systems that do not contain galvanized steel, except that the pH restriction does not 
apply.

a continuous basis using automated control and feed equipment. The concentration of 
these formulated products varies greatly from vendor to vendor. Biocides are usually, 
but not always, liquid products. It is common to use an oxidizing biocide as a primary 
biocide and a non-oxidizing biocide as a secondary biocide, used as needed to control 
bacteria and other biological growth. Oxidizing biocides can either be fed continuously 
at a low level or dosed periodically at a higher level. Non-oxidizers are dosed as needed 
and only when oxidizing biocides are either ineffective or not used at all. 
 
4-6.6.2 
Testing. Testing should be done regularly to insure that COC, chemical 
levels, and bacteria levels are within the targeted control range. This requirement could 
demand a testing frequency of 3 times per week, or even daily. 
 
4-6.7 
Cooling Tower Operator Duties. If detected early, problems associated 
with scaling, corrosion and fouling in a cooling tower system can be minimized by 
corrective action. Some of the things the operator should look for when on-site are 
described below. 
 
Parameter 
Approach 
COC 
Target a minimum of 3 COC (ideally 5 COC) that the 
chemical treatment will allow. 
Corrosion control 
1. Use of cathodic corrosion, possibly supplemented with 
anodic inhibitors for mild steel. If a galvanized cooling tower 
is present, use a polysilicate or low-level phosphate while 
keeping pH in the range of 8 to 9. 
2. Copper corrosion inhibitor should be used for all copper 
tubes and especially for enhanced and super-enhanced 
copper tubing. 
Scale control 
Phosphonate/polymer program, augmented by a phosphate 
dispersant if phosphate corrosion inhibitor is used. 
SS 
Polymer dispersant coupled with adequate flow. Avoid no-
flow conditions in heat exchangers as much as possible. 
Mechanical filtration and routine physical sump cleaning 
recommended. 
Microbiological 
control 
1. Primary biocide: oxidizing biocide using continuous feed or 
slug feed as an alternate. 
2. Secondary biocide: non-oxidizing biocide using slug feed, 
as required.

4-6.7.1 
Cooling Tower Distribution Deck. It is important to look for the presence 
of algae, debris, or anything that has plugged water distribution holes causing an 
uneven water flow through the tower, thus lowering tower efficiency. Clean plugged 
holes and replace damaged water distribution spray nozzles. 
 
 
In addition, look for the presence of algae deposits. If algae deposits are 
present, increase the level or frequency of biocide or algaecide treatment, and cover the 
deck if uncovered. 
4-6.7.2 
Cooling Tower Fill, Air Intake Slats, and Basin 
 
4-6.7.2.1 
Scale Deposits on Cooling Tower Fill. The presence of deposits, 
particularly on cooling tower fill, can be established by removing some fill to determine if 
partial plugging has occurred. Scale can range in color from white to gray or reddish 
depending on the scale composition. Scale formation on the cooling tower fill usually 
indicates a severe scaling situation. If possible, obtain a sample of the scale for analysis 
and, based on the result, select a scale inhibitor for that specific scale. 
 
4-6.7.2.2 
Scale Deposits on Air Intake Slats. Scale can form on the air intake 
slats of a cooling tower. This buildup is due mostly to water splashing and evaporating, 
causing deposition of soluble salts or minerals. This situation does not indicate a serious 
problem. These deposits can be, and should be, washed off periodically, but ideally not 
into the cooling tower basin. Chemical treatment can provide some reduction in the 
occurrence deposits. 
 
4-6.7.2.3 
Slime Deposits. Slime deposits (microbiological) can sometimes be 
detected by feeling below the water level on the distribution deck and on the walls of the 
cooling tower basin. Most microbiological growth will have a slimy feel. If slime deposits 
are present, increase biocide frequency or increase the dosage. 
 
4-6.7.2.4 
Suspended Solids. The purpose of a dispersant is to keep particulate 
solids in suspension and to prevent them from settling or from adhering to heat transfer 
surfaces. Adequate water flow is required to prevent them from settling. Particulate 
solids in suspension are removed with the blowdown water. The tower water should be 
turbid if the dispersant is doing its job. Keep the cooling tower sump clean of SS by 
cleaning periodically and using a filter.

note and record the visual appearance with regard to the presence of scale, rust, or 
biomass. Take photographs of the corrosion coupons. Submit (or evaluate) coupons for 
corrosion rate and for the type of corrosion that is occurring.

inside (water-contacted) surfaces of heat exchanger tubes, a boroscope is needed 
because only a few inches of the interior can be seen visually using a flashlight. Scale

The Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, and Fluid Flow Fundamentals Handbook was

personnel, and the technical staff with the necessary fundamentals training to ensure a basic

OVERVIEW
The Department of Energy Fundamentals Handbook entitled Thermodynamics, Heat
Transfer, and Fluid Flow was prepared as an information resource for personnel who are
responsible for the operation of the Department's nuclear facilities.  A basic understanding of the
thermal sciences is necessary for DOE nuclear facility operators, maintenance personnel, and the
technical staff to safely operate and maintain the facility and facility support systems.  The
information in the handbook is presented to provide a foundation for applying engineering
concepts to the job.  This knowledge will help personnel more fully understand the impact that
their actions may have on the safe and reliable operation of facility components and systems.

that are contained in three volumes.  The following is a brief description of the information
presented in each module of the handbook.

affected by various processes.  The module also explains how energy balances can

pH Effluent limitations under

(a) Where a permittee continuously 
measures the pH of wastewater pursu-
ant to a requirement or option in a Na-
tional Pollutant Discharge Elimination 
System (NPDES) permit issued pursu-
ant to section 402 of the Act, the per-
mittee shall maintain the pH of such 
wastewater within the range set forth 
in the applicable effluent limitations 
guidelines, except excursions from the 
range are permitted subject to the fol-
lowing limitations: 
(1) The total time during which the 
pH values are outside the required 
range of pH values shall not exceed 7 
hours and 26 minutes in any calendar 
month; and 
(2) No individual excursion from the 
range of pH values shall exceed 60 min-
utes. 
(b) The Director, as defined in § 122.3 
of this chapter, may adjust the require-
ments set forth in paragraph (a) of this 
section with respect to the length of 
individual excursions from the range of 
pH values, if a different period of time 
is appropriate based upon the treat-
ment system, plant configuration or 
other technical factors. 
(c) For purposes of this section, an 
excursion is an unintentional and tem-
porary incident in which the pH value 
of discharge wastewater exceeds the 
range set forth in the applicable efflu-
ent limitations guidelines.

import math
import numpy as np

# Roughness in ft from 23 21 16 cl. 2.2
roughness = {
    'CS': 0.00015,
    'GALV': 0.0005,
    'CU': 0.000005,
    'HOSE': 0.0008,
}
nu = 1.08e-5
g = 32.174

def colebrook_f(Re, e_over_D):
    if Re < 2000:
        return 64.0 / Re
    f = 0.02
    for _ in range(50):
        rhs = -2.0 * math.log10(e_over_D / 3.7 + 2.51 / (Re * math.sqrt(f)))
        f = 1.0 / (rhs * rhs)
    return f

def run_head_loss(Q_gpm, id_in, L_ft, sum_LD, mat):
    D_ft = id_in / 12.0
    A_ft2 = math.pi * D_ft * D_ft / 4.0
    Q_cfs = Q_gpm / (60.0 * 1728.0 / 231.0)
    v = Q_cfs / A_ft2
    Re = v * D_ft / nu
    f = colebrook_f(Re, roughness[mat] / D_ft)
    h = f * (L_ft / D_ft + sum_LD) * (v * v) / (2.0 * g)
    return h, v, Re, f

[  1] Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
[  2] 1.1   SUMMARY
[  3] This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
[  4] The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
[  5] Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
[  6] 1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
[  7] UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
[  8] DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
[  9] 40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
[ 10] 29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.

[ 12] 1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
[ 13] Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
[ 14] Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
[ 15]   a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
[ 16]   b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
[ 17]   c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
[ 18]   d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
[ 19] 1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
[ 20] Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
[ 21] Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
[ 22] The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
[ 23]     GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
[ 24] where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
[ 25] The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
[ 26] 3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
[ 27] Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
[ 28] For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
[ 29] a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
[ 30] b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
[ 31]        1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
[ 32]    with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
[ 33] c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
[ 34]        h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
[ 35] d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
[ 36] e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
[ 37] f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
[ 38] 3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
[ 39] The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
[ 40]   a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
[ 41]   b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
[ 42] The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
[ 43] NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
[ 44] Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.
[ 45] 3.4   CHEMICAL CLEANING
[ 46] Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
[ 47] The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
[ 48] Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
[ 49] Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
[ 50] That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
[ 51] Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.
[ 52] 3.5   PASSIVATION AND TREATMENT PROGRAM
[ 53] Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
[ 54] Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
[ 55] Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
[ 56] Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
[ 57] That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
[ 58] Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
[ 59] Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.
[ 60] 3.6   RINSE DISPLACEMENT MODEL
[ 61] The number of rinse displacements required after chemical cleaning shall be computed from the project displacement model:
[ 62]        C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n)
[ 63] where C_n is the circuit water conductivity after n full circuit-volume displacements, C_mk is the makeup water conductivity from SW-02, C_0 is the conductivity of the spent cleaning solution from VD-06, n is the number of displacements of the circuit FLUSH volume (pipework plus the hold-up of components that are NOT bypassed), and eta is the mixing efficiency of the circuit:
[ 64]        eta = 0.45 for a circuit that contains a parallel cold-plate manifold bank or coil bank, that is, a circuit any of whose components Schedule M-602 describes as a cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank
[ 65]        eta = 0.62 for every other circuit
[ 66] n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
[ 67] That criterion states the rinse pH as a tolerance and as a window in one sentence. BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
[ 68] Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
[ 69] A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.
[ 70] 3.7   DISCHARGE
[ 71] All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.
[ 72] Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.
[ 73] The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
[ 74] 3.8   TURNOVER
[ 75] Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. Declare the method used for each circuit in the plan, as turnover_method. Then recirculate for not less than the period the governing water-treatment criteria document requires before sampling, and sample while circulating.
[ 76]   RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP - the passivation charge is retained in the circuit and the circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge. Permitted only where the maintenance residual of the selected program is not below its passivation residual, so that the top-up raises rather than dilutes the inhibitor level.
[ 77]   DRAIN_AND_REFILL - the passivation charge is drained to the route declared for it and the circuit is refilled to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge.
[ 78] REPORTING CONVENTION. On every chemistry row, target_ppm is the ABSOLUTE residual the circuit is to be held at, and product_quantity is the quantity the dose ADDS. Under RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP those differ: the top-up adds only the difference between the maintenance residual and the residual the retained charge already carries. Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.

SECTION 23 25 16 - PROCESS COOLING WATER CLEANING, FLUSHING AND PASSIVATION
Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
1.1   SUMMARY
This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.
Section 23 21 16 for pipe materials, roughness and the hydrostatic test regime.
1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
  a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
  b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
  c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
  d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
    GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
       1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
   with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
       h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
  a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
  b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.
3.4   CHEMICAL CLEANING
Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.
3.5   PASSIVATION AND TREATMENT PROGRAM
Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.
3.6   RINSE DISPLACEMENT MODEL
The number of rinse displacements required after chemical cleaning shall be computed from the project displacement model:
       C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n)
where C_n is the circuit water conductivity after n full circuit-volume displacements, C_mk is the makeup water conductivity from SW-02, C_0 is the conductivity of the spent cleaning solution from VD-06, n is the number of displacements of the circuit FLUSH volume (pipework plus the hold-up of components that are NOT bypassed), and eta is the mixing efficiency of the circuit:
       eta = 0.45 for a circuit that contains a parallel cold-plate manifold bank or coil bank, that is, a circuit any of whose components Schedule M-602 describes as a cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank
       eta = 0.62 for every other circuit
n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
That criterion states the rinse pH as a tolerance and as a window in one sentence. BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.
3.7   DISCHARGE
All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.
Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.
The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
3.8   TURNOVER
Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. Declare the method used for each circuit in the plan, as turnover_method. Then recirculate for not less than the period the governing water-treatment criteria document requires before sampling, and sample while circulating.
  RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP - the passivation charge is retained in the circuit and the circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge. Permitted only where the maintenance residual of the selected program is not below its passivation residual, so that the top-up raises rather than dilutes the inhibitor level.
  DRAIN_AND_REFILL - the passivation charge is drained to the route declared for it and the circuit is refilled to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge.
REPORTING CONVENTION. On every chemistry row, target_ppm is the ABSOLUTE residual the circuit is to be held at, and product_quantity is the quantity the dose ADDS. Under RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP those differ: the top-up adds only the difference between the maintenance residual and the residual the retained charge already carries. Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.
Where two tabulated inhibitors are carried at once - an inhibitor and a copper azole, for instance - and their tabulated pH bands overlap only in part, control to the INTERSECTION of the two bands, which satisfies both.
3.9   WATER AND EFFLUENT ACCOUNTING
Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. State both figures for every stage in the plan.
    hydrostatic test (where one is owed)   draw V_f              effluent V_f
    initial flush                          draw n_f x V_f        effluent n_f x V_f
    chemical cleaning                      draw V_f              effluent V_f
    rinse                                  draw (n_r - c) x V_f  effluent (n_r - 1) x V_f - d
    passivation charge                     draw 0                effluent 0
    film-formation hold                    draw 0                effluent 0
    turnover, RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP            draw V_s - V_f        effluent 0
    turnover, DRAIN_AND_REFILL             draw V_s              effluent V_f
The circuit is left FULL at the end of the last rinse displacement, so that displacement is not drained: that is why the rinse effluent is one displacement less than the rinse draw.
The passivation charge is dosed into the water standing in the circuit at the end of the rinse; it is not a fresh fill.
A rinse that takes one cascaded displacement and draws the rest from the metered supply is a single row with a single water_source: declare it CASCADE_FROM:<donor circuit>. The makeup balance above already accounts for the other displacements being drawn fresh.
d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume. A circuit may donate to at most one receiver and receive from at most one donor, and a donor's FLUSH volume must be not less than its receiver's, or it cannot fill it.
These figures balance: over the programme, water drawn equals effluent produced plus the SYSTEM volume left standing in every circuit at turnover.
Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity in that day (SW-01 cl.2).
3.10   COST BASIS
Price the programme on the following basis, and report the total and its breakdown in the plan.
  a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each unit-day between the circuits that held that unit that day IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS each held it inside the day, merging any overlap within a circuit. The share so obtained is a real number and is NOT rounded; the whole day is charged once and divided. Two circuits that share a unit-day therefore pay a part each, and a circuit whose work is spread thinly across many days pays for every one of them.
  b. Commissioning crew: a crew is ENGAGED BY THE SHIFT, not by the circuit. Each crew is charged ONE shift rate for every 12-hour SHIFT [12k, 12k+12) hours from mobilisation in which it attends anything at all, counted ONCE however many circuits it attends in it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each crew-shift between the circuits attended in it IN PROPORTION TO THE ATTENDED HOURS each took inside the shift; the share is a real number a

Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.

Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume.   a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. A stage lasts as long as its activities OCCUPY: its duration is the SUM of the hours of the activities scheduled for it, and an idle gap between two of them is no part of it.        initial flush           n_f x V_f at the declared flow
       chemical cleaning       the greater of the required circulation time and V_f at the declared flow
       rinse                   n_r x V_f at the declared flow
       passivation charge      V_f at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
       turnover                the fill volume of the declared method at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
     An unattended film-formation hold, and unattended standby inside a longer scheduled occupancy, are not charged (SW-01 cl.3, 01 91 13 cl.1.7); a stage with no attended time opens no shift. A crew attends one activity at a time and a rented unit serves one circuit at a time, so no crew may be charged with more than 12 attended hours in a shift and no unit held for more than 24 hours in a day.
     WHAT a AND b MEAN FOR THE PROGRAMME. Both lines are bought by the period, so the two of them price the SEQUENCE, not the circuit: a programme that dovetails its circuits into the same unit-days and the same crew-shifts pays a fraction of what the same engineering costs when the circuits are run one after another. Neither line can be worked out from one circuit in isolation, and a circuit's share of both moves when another circuit's schedule moves. Against that pull stands cl.3.9 and SW-01 cl.2: the site's daily water allocation is shared too, so drawing the whole programme into a few days buys the excess at the trucked rate, and the cascade links of cl.3.6 force the circuits they join to rinse in sequence. The economic plan is the one that settles those against each other.
  c. Water: metered rate up to the daily allocation and the trucked rate above it (SW-01 cl.1, cl.2). APPORTIONMENT: the allocation is a site-wide meter, so form ONE programme-wide average rate - the metered and trucked volumes priced at their own rates, divided by the total volume drawn - and apply that single rate to every circuit's draw. Do not attempt to attribute particular gallons to particular circuits.
  d. Effluent: the sewer rate for volume to the metered connection, the tanker rate for volume remove

[66] n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.

BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
[68] Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
[69] A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.

[71] All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.

[73] The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
[74] 3.8   TURNOVER
[75] Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. 5-3.6 
Cooling Water Fouling. 
The term “fouling” refers to the deposition of materials that are normally held in 
suspension in the cooling water: mud, silt, and other SS brought into the system with 
the makeup water; dust, dirt, and debris scrubbed out of the air passing through the 
tower; product leakage such as oils; corrosion products from the system; and biological 
organisms, both living and dead. Combinations of any or all of these materials can be 
present in the cooling water. 
5-3.7 
Fouling Control. 
Fouling from mud, dirt, and corrosion products can be controlled by the addition of a 
water-soluble polymer dispersant, such as a polyacrylate. The addition of about 4 to 5 
ppm of active polymer, together with sufficient water velocity (3.28 feet per second (1 
meter per second)), can keep foulants in suspension and prevent them from being 
deposited on heat transfer surfaces. Higher dosages (5 to 20 ppm) of active polymer 
can be required for heavily fouled systems. It is best to reduce the loading of SS by 
mechanically removing them from the system through blowdown, filtration, and physical 
sump cleaning. Removing oil or oily materials requires a non-foaming surfactant. 
Paragraph 5-4 describes prevention of fouling by biological organisms. Table 5-2 
summarizes foulant control methods.

Large biological organisms such as clams, snails, mussels, or similar species are 
referred to as macrobiological organisms. The presence of any biological growth can be 
detrimental to cooling tower operations. Problems include fouling, corrosion, and loss of

These problems can lead to downtime, higher operating cost, and even premature 
replacement of equipment. Additionally, some bacteria are pathogenic and can pose a 
risk to human life.

Algae. 
The term “algae” refers to algal, microbiological, tiny, stringy blue and blue-green plants, 
which are usually found growing in masses on top of and on sides of cooling towers.

5-7 
COOLING WATER SYSTEM START-UP AND LAYUP 
REQUIREMENTS. 
The startup of a new cooling water system requires special consideration. Proper 
cooling water system layup is also important, especially for chiller tube bundles or other 
heat exchange equipment. For a new cooling tower system, it is important to make sure 
that the equipment that contacts the cooling water is clean and properly protected from 
initial corrosion. Also, disinfection is needed to eliminate the presence of microbiological 
organisms that can cause corrosion, deposits, and growth of pathogenic organisms 
such as Legionella bacteria. Implementation of a proper layup process is critical to 
prevent corrosion and microbiological growth during stagnant water conditions. 
5-7.1 
Stand-by Conditions. 
The term “stand-by” is often applied to a chiller that is in rotation with other chillers on-
line. This stand-by period could be of varying duration, from a few days to a few weeks. 
Rotating chillers frequently is important for minimizing stagnant conditions that lead to 
under-deposit and MIC corrosion. It is good practice to run the recirculation pumps 
through a stand-by chiller for at least 15 minutes each day to minimize corrosion. A 
chiller that must be left on stand-by for an extended period of weeks without 
recirculation should be laid up wet or dry according to procedures described in 
paragraph 5-7.4. 
5-7.2 
Common Problems during Layup or Due to Improper Initial Start-up. 
Common problems that occur during layup or due to improper initial start-up include 
corrosion of tubes and transfer piping (sometimes to the point of failure), micro- 
biological growth with potential for MIC corrosion, and growth of pathogenic 
microorganisms. 
5-7.3 
Start-up of New Cooling Water Tower Systems. 
5-7.3.1 
Initial Cleaning. 
A new cooling water tower system will contain dirt, oils, greasy films, and rust located on 
the metal surfaces as a result of system fabrication. A pre-operational alkaline cleaning 
process is required to remove the dirt, oil, grease, and rust, and to prepare metal 
surfaces for initial corrosion control. When galvanized steel is involved, special care 
must be taken so that the pH does not exceed 8.5 during the cleaning and passivation 
process to avoid conditions that promote white rust. The cleaning and passivating 
procedure for a new cooling tower system is usually part of a new system construction 
project and, as such, is not in the direct control of the cooling system operations 
personnel. Verification of the completion of these important steps is obtained from the 
contracting officer involved with the project. A cleaning and passivation procedure for 
cooling tower systems with galvanized steel is provided below. The procedure is similar 
for systems that do not contain galvanized steel, except that the pH restriction does not 
apply.

Cleaning and Passivation Procedures. 
In the startup of new cooling tower systems containing complex metallurgies that 
include galvanized steel, follow the cleaning and passivation procedures for cooling 
tower systems containing galvanized steel, stainless steel, mild steel, or copper. These 
procedures should not be used for cleaning and passivating aluminum. Conventional 
chemical cleaners and typical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) water 
treatment programs use highly alkaline, high-pH water, which can initiate white rust

Algae grow only in sunlit areas. They will slough off and become part of the suspended 
matter in the circulating water, a situation which may cause fouling and plugging of 
water sprays. Algae also provide a breeding place, and are a nutrient, for bacteria. 
5-4.2 
Bacteria. 
The term “bacteria” refers to a large group of one-celled microorganisms. Bacteria can 
grow in either the absence or presence of sunlight. There are several ways to classify 
bacteria, including “aerobic,” meaning those living in the presence of oxygen, and 
“anaerobic,” meaning those living in the absence of oxygen. In a cooling water system, 
one can categorize bacteria as either “planktonic” or “sessile,” which are terms that 
describe whether the bacteria are, respectively, either free floating or found growing on 
surfaces (stickers). Categories of bacteria are described below. Table 5-3 shows types 
of bacteria and their growth conditions. 
5-4.2.1 
Planktonic Bacteria. 
Planktonic bacteria are suspended in the water, sometimes referred to as “free floaters” 
or “swimmers,” and are aerobic bacteria that thrive in an oxygenated environment. They 
are not harmful to the cooling system since they do not cause deposits or corrosion, but 
they can provide nutrients for other microorganisms; in addition, some planktonic 
bacteria such as Legionella Pneumophila are pathogenic and can present a significant 
human health risk. 
5-4.2.2 
Sessile Bacteria. 
Sessile bacteria are stickers, or non-swimming bacteria, and can cause deposits and 
corrosion. Sessile bacteria types include slime-formers and anaerobic (corrosive) 
bacteria. Slime-formers can grow and form gelatinous deposits on almost any surface in 
contact with the cooling water. These deposits can grow so large that they restrict water 
flow and interfere with heat transfer; they also may promote under-deposit corrosion. 
Feeling the sides of the cooling tower basin just below the water level is one way to 
detect the presence of slime-formers. Usually if there are slime formers in the system, 
you can feel deposits. Anaerobic bacteria thrive in oxygen- deprived environments and 
often establish colonies beneath slime deposits or under other types of deposits. One 
type of anaerobe is sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB), which produce hydrogen sulfide, a 
chemical that is very corrosive to metals. This type of corrosion attack is much localized 
and can result in pipe and tube failures. The presence of SRB should be suspected in a 
water system if the underside of a slime layer is black or if you detect the odor of rotten 
eggs. Any type of microbiological corrosion is referred to as microbiologically influenced 
corrosion (MIC). Bacteria cause most of the MIC found in cooling water systems. Use 
surface microbiological measurements to monitor sessile bacteria.

The term “microbiological control” refers to techniques used to minimize the presence of 
microbiological organisms in cooling water. Chemical biocide treatment is the method 
used on government installations for microbiological control in cooling water. Biocides 
that are used to control microbiological growth fall into one of two broad categories: 
oxidizing and non-oxidizing microbiocides. A cost-effective approach for control involves 
the regular use of oxidizers as a primary biocide, augmented by selective use of non-
oxidizing biocides. Important factors for the effectiveness of any biocide include using a 
proper dosage and allowing adequate contact time with the microbiological organisms. 
All microbiocides are toxic and must be handled safely and with caution; use the SDS 
for safety instructions.
